---
title: Paper template
---

The group has a LaTeX template for journal articles in the
[paper-template](https://github.com/tolborg-group/paper-template) repository.
It uses [Pixi](pixi.qmd) to install LaTeX, such that the only prerequisite for
compiling a paper is that Pixi is installed, and it uses GitHub Actions to
compile the PDF on every push.

Compared to Overleaf, the paper is an ordinary git repository on our own
machine. We write in the editor we prefer, the document compiles offline, the
scripts that produce the figures are kept next to the text, and co-authors
contribute through git as they would for code.

This page describes how the template is used. The
[README](https://github.com/tolborg-group/paper-template#readme) of the
repository is the reference for the details.

## Starting a paper

Clone the template into a directory named after the paper and disconnect it
from the template repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tolborg-group/paper-template.git my-paper
cd my-paper
git remote remove origin
```

The paper then needs its own repository on GitHub. With the
[GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) a private repository is created and the
paper pushed to it with

```bash
gh repo create tolborg-group/my-paper --private --source . --push
```

## Building the PDF

The paper is compiled with

```bash
pixi run build
```

which writes `main.pdf` to the root of the repository. While writing, it is
more convenient to let the PDF be rebuilt whenever a `.tex` or `.bib` file is
saved:

```bash
pixi run watch
```

The template compiles with [Tectonic](https://tectonic-typesetting.github.io),
which downloads the LaTeX packages a document uses the first time they are
needed. The first build therefore takes a few minutes and requires an internet
connection, while later builds are fast and work offline. A new package is
used by adding the `\usepackage` line; nothing has to be installed by hand.

LaTeX lives in its own environment, named `latex`, which Pixi selects
automatically for these tasks, see [Environments](pixi.qmd#environments).

## Layout

```
main.tex            preamble, title, author list and the order of the sections
sections/           one file per section
figures/            the figures and the scripts that produce them
references.bib      the BibTeX database
pixi.toml           the environments and tasks
.github/workflows/  the CI build
```

Each section is its own file, which keeps the differences between versions
small and makes it easier for several authors to work at the same time.

`main.tex` defines two commands for communicating between authors: `\todo{…}`
renders in red and `\note{…}` in blue. Both should be gone before submission.
The remaining writing conventions, e.g. the use of `siunitx` and `cleveref`,
are listed in the README.

## Target journal

The template is set up for Physical Review Letters through REVTeX 4-2. Other
APS journals only require a different class option in the first line of
`main.tex`, e.g. `prb` instead of `prl`. For ACS journals the document class is
replaced by `achemso`, and most other publishers supply a `.cls` file that is
placed in the root of the repository. The README has the details.

## Figures

The figures used by LaTeX are committed to `figures/` together with the Python
scripts that generate them, such that every figure in the paper can be traced
back to, and regenerated from, its script. The scripts run in the default
environment:

```bash
pixi run python figures/kpoint-convergence.py
```

This environment has `matplotlib` and `pandas`. Other packages are added with
`pixi add`, see [Adding packages](pixi.qmd#adding-packages).

## The PDF on GitHub

Every push to `main` and every pull request compiles the paper on GitHub, and
the PDF is kept for 30 days as an artifact of that run. It is found under the
**Actions** tab of the repository, or downloaded with `gh run download`. This
allows a co-author to read the current state of the paper without compiling
it, and it shows immediately when a change has broken the build.

A version that should be kept, e.g. the one that was submitted, is marked with
a tag that starts with `v`:

```bash
git tag v1.0-submitted
git push origin v1.0-submitted
```

This creates a release on GitHub with the PDF attached.

## Help from Claude

Two of the [group skills](../ai/skills.qmd) are useful when working with the
template: `/latex:diagnose` finds out why a document does not compile, and
`/git:sync` commits, pulls and pushes for those who do not use git daily.
